content: The Mississippi Embayment is a distinct physiographic feature located in the south-central region of the United States. It represents a northward extension of fluvial sediments originating from the Mississippi River Delta, extending to its confluence with the Ohio River at Cairo, Illinois. This embayment is characterized as a topographically low-lying basin filled with sediments that range in age from the Cretaceous period to more recent times. At its northern end, the embayment exhibits an unusual geological discontinuity, where Paleozoic sedimentary rocks are found both to the east in Kentucky and Tennessee and to the west in Missouri and Arkansas. The current sedimentary basin formed as a result of the infilling of a tectonic basin that originated during the Cretaceous period. During the Cretaceous through the early Tertiary periods, this area existed as a large bay along the ancient shoreline. The northern end of the embayment is also notable for being the location of the New Madrid Seismic Zone, which was the site of the significant New Madrid earthquakes of 1811–1812. The region is underlain by geologically anomalous features, including the Reelfoot Rift, an ancient failed continental rift that dates back to the Precambrian breakup of the supercontinent Rodinia. The later opening of the Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf of Mexico during the late Paleozoic to early Mesozoic breakup of Pangaea likely influenced and may have partially reactivated this ancient rift. The formation of the Mississippi Embayment is linked to a break in what was once a continuous mountain range, which included the modern Appalachian range running along the Atlantic coast and the Ouachita range running west of the Mississippi River. This ancestral Appalachian-Ouachita range was uplifted approximately 300 million years ago when the tectonic plate carrying North America collided with the plates carrying South America and Africa, forming the supercontinent Pangaea. To explain how part of this mountain range became a basin, Roy B. Van Arsdale and Randel Cox of the University of Memphis proposed a detailed explanation in the January 2007 issue of Scientific American. As Pangaea began to break apart around 95 million years ago, North America passed over a volcanic hotspot in the Earth's mantle, specifically the Bermuda hotspot, which was undergoing intense activity. The upwelling of magma from this hotspot caused further uplift of a portion of the Appalachian-Ouachita range, forming an arch that reached a height of approximately 2–3 kilometers. This uplift was followed by subsidence, creating a trough that was subsequently flooded by the Gulf of Mexico. As sea levels dropped, the Mississippi River and other rivers extended their courses into the embayment, gradually filling it with sediment. Evidence supporting the Van Arsdale-Cox explanation includes the presence of seismic zones centered on New Madrid, Missouri, and Charleston, South Carolina, both of which were sources of devastating 19th-century earthquakes. Additional evidence is found in diamond-bearing kimberlite pipes in Arkansas, which are products of volcanic activity associated with the region's complex geological history.
